findings.title: Memory Pressure and OOM History
findings.explanation:
Over the last 10 / 60 / 300 seconds, at least one program was stalled waiting for memory 0.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% of the time, and all programs were stalled at once 0.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% of the time.

No meaningful stalls at the moment: programs are getting the memory they ask for without waiting.

The kernel has killed 1 process since boot because memory ran out. This counts both a whole machine out of RAM and a program or service exceeding its own memory limit (a container or systemd MemoryMax).
findings.recommendation:
1. Confirm what is happening now (the pressure file should be near zero on a healthy machine; in vmstat, non-zero si/so columns mean active swapping):
    cat /proc/pressure/memory
    vmstat 1 5
2. Find out who was killed and why (the log says whether the whole machine or a single memory limit was the cause):
    sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'out of memory|oom-kill|killed process'
3. Reduce the demand: qemu-system-x86 holds the most private memory (96.6 GB). The Used memory page lists the consumers and what to do about each.
4. There is no swap, so the kernel has nothing to relieve the pressure with. The Swap configuration finding has the zram and swap file commands.
5. Stop one runaway service from taking the whole machine down by giving it a ceiling (MemoryHigh slows it first, MemoryMax is the hard limit), and shield the services that must survive with a negative OOM score:
    sudo systemctl set-property <service> MemoryHigh=<N>G MemoryMax=<M>G
    sudo systemctl edit <critical-service>     # add: [Service] OOMScoreAdjust=-900
6. Let a userspace daemon act early, while the machine is still responsive, instead of waiting for the kernel's OOM killer. systemd-oomd needs systemd 248+ and cgroup v2; earlyoom is the alternative that works anywhere:
    sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-oomd
    sudo apt install earlyoom && sudo systemctl enable --now earlyoom

findings.title: Memory Usage Overview
findings.explanation:
Of 247.5 GB of RAM, 160.5 GB (64.8%) is in use by programs and the kernel, and 87.1 GB (35.2%) is available for new allocations without swapping — comfortable. These are the 'used' and 'available' columns of free(1).

Only 15.8 GB is completely unused, and that is normal: Linux fills spare RAM with cache and hands it back the moment a program asks. free(1) shows 73.4 GB as 'buff/cache', but that figure includes 427 MB of shared memory (tmpfs, /dev/shm, graphics buffers) which stays in RAM; the part the kernel can genuinely give back is 73.0 GB.

What matters is 'available', not 'free'. The Used memory, Page cache, Shared memory, Swap, Pressure and Kernel tuning pages break this number down.

findings.explanation:
160.5 GB of RAM (64.8%) is in use and 87.1 GB (35.2%) is available — comfortable.

Where the 247.5 GB of RAM goes right now:
  Programs (private memory)         112.0 GB   45.3%
  Page cache (files)                 68.3 GB   27.6%
  Buffers                             1.5 GB    0.6%
  Reclaimable kernel caches           3.2 GB    1.3%
  Kernel memory (not reclaimable)     2.3 GB    0.9%
  Free                               15.8 GB    6.4%
  ZFS ARC cache                      41.0 GB   16.6%
  Not attributed                      2.5 GB    1.0%
  Smaller items (each under 0.5%)     972 MB    0.4%

About 115.3 GB (46.6%) of RAM is memory that cannot simply be dropped: programs' private memory (it can only be swapped out), shared memory, non-reclaimable kernel memory and reserved huge pages. The rest is cache the kernel can take back on demand.

Largest consumers by private memory (each page is counted once, so programs that share libraries are not inflated):

  2. Isolated Web Co (22 processes) — 4.9 GB private (2.0% of RAM)
  3. AppRun.wrapped — 3.4 GB private, 43 MB file-backed, 4 kB shared (1.4% of RAM)
  4. fwupd — 849 MB private, 34 MB file-backed (0.3% of RAM)
  5. gnome-shell — 810 MB private, 151 MB file-backed, 24 kB shared (0.3% of RAM)

findings.title: Page Cache
findings.explanation:
The page cache holds 68.3 GB (27.6% of RAM): copies of files recently read or written, kept so the next access is served from memory instead of the disk. Disk-block buffers add 1.5 GB.

64.3 GB of the file cache has not been touched recently (the kernel drops that first) and 5.5 GB is in active use. Running programs map 2.2 GB of it.

Reclaimable kernel caches (the dentry and inode caches that remember file names and metadata) add 3.2 GB.

This memory is not wasted: it makes file access fast and is handed back to programs the moment they ask for it.

A large cache is therefore a sign of a healthy machine, not a leak. Emptying it (echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) frees nothing of lasting value: it only forces files to be read from the disk again and slows everything down until the cache is rebuilt. It is a benchmarking tool, not an optimisation.

ZFS keeps its own cache (the ARC) outside the page cache; it is described under Kernel memory.

findings.title: Dirty Page / Writeback Pressure
findings.explanation:
161 MB is waiting to be written to disk (0.2% of what can be dirtied), comfortably below the background threshold of 8.6 GB.

Background writeback starts at 8.6 GB and writers are slowed from 12.8 GB; the hard limit is 17.1 GB. These are measured against 85.5 GB (free memory plus file cache).

On this machine the ratio settings allow up to 17.1 GB of dirty data to pile up before writers are blocked. Flushing that much at once can freeze programs for many seconds on a slow disk; many administrators cap it with fixed byte limits instead.
findings.recommendation:
1. Optional: cap the amount of dirty data with fixed limits (256 MB to start background writeback, 1 GB before writers block). Setting the byte values replaces the ratios:
    sudo sysctl vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456 vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824
    printf 'vm.dirty_background_bytes = 268435456\nvm.dirty_bytes = 1073741824\n' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-dirty.conf

findings.title: Shared Memory Usage
findings.explanation:
Shared memory takes 427 MB of RAM (0.2%), a normal level. It is the part of the 'buff/cache' figure of free(1) that is not really cache: it stays in RAM until deleted.

Where it lives — tmpfs mounts (files that exist only in RAM):
  1. /run — 18 MB of 49.5 GB (0.0% full)
  2. /run/user/1000 — 16 MB of 24.8 GB (0.1% full)
  3. /dev/shm — 8 MB of 80.0 GB (0.0% full)

SysV shared memory: 17 segments using 40 MB of RAM. 37 MB of it belongs to segments that running programs are attached to — memory in legitimate use, such as a database's buffer pool.

1 SysV segment (3 MB resident) has no program attached. The program that created it has exited or crashed without removing it, so the memory stays allocated until the segment is deleted:
  - id 3309607 — 4 MB (3 MB resident), owner uid 1000

Largest shared mappings per program (programs that share the same memory each count it, so do not add these up):
  1. nautilus (PID 1881039) — 97 MB
  2. firefox-esr (PID 2438007) — 55 MB
  3. Xwayland (PID 11849) — 41 MB

findings.title: Kernel Swappiness Setting
findings.explanation:
vm.swappiness is 10 (kernel default 60). It decides how eagerly the kernel moves idle program memory to swap instead of dropping file cache: low values protect programs' memory, high values protect the file cache. The scale runs from 0 to 200.

No swap is configured, so there is nowhere to move program memory and this setting has no effect on it. See Swap configuration.

findings.title: Swap Configuration
findings.explanation:
Swap: none configured.

No swap is configured. Without it the kernel can only reclaim file cache; once that is gone, the only option left is the OOM killer. Even a small swap lets idle program memory move out of the way and gives a memory spike somewhere to go. (Exceptions: Kubernetes nodes, where the kubelet expects swap off by default, and appliances that deliberately prefer an OOM kill to slowness.)
findings.recommendation:
1. Preferred: compressed RAM swap (zram). It needs no disk space, causes no disk wear and is much faster than swap on a disk. This sets it to half of RAM, kept after reboot:
    sudo apt install systemd-zram-generator     # Fedora, Arch, openSUSE: zram-generator
    printf '[zram0]\nzram-size = ram / 2\ncompression-algorithm = zstd\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
    sudo systemctl start systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service
2. Or a swap file of 8 GB on disk (ext4 or xfs; on Btrfs use 'btrfs filesystem mkswapfile' instead of fallocate):
    sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
    sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
    sudo mkswap /swapfile
    sudo swapon /swapfile
    echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab   # keep it after reboot

findings.title: Kernel Memory
findings.explanation:
The kernel itself holds 6.1 GB of RAM (2.5%): 5.5 GB of slab caches (3.2 GB reclaimable, 2.3 GB not), 354 MB of page tables, 50 MB of kernel stacks and 141 MB of per-CPU data. This memory belongs to no program; it is the cost of running the system.

ZFS is loaded. Its cache (the ARC) holds 41.0 GB (16.6% of RAM, limit 246.5 GB). ZFS allocates it itself, outside the page cache, and /proc/meminfo's 'available' figure does not count it — so a ZFS machine always looks fuller than it is. ZFS does give the memory back when programs ask, but more slowly than the page cache does.

vm.min_free_kbytes is 88 MB: the reserve the kernel keeps free so it can always satisfy urgent allocations.

96.6 GB of RAM (39.0%) is locked and can never be swapped or reclaimed (mlock, ramfs, memory held by some drivers). 96.6 GB of it is locked by programs with mlock.

findings.title: Memory Overcommit Policy
findings.explanation: Overcommit is in heuristic mode (the default): the kernel lets programs reserve more memory than exists and refuses only absurd single requests. Programs have reserved 127.2 GB of address space (51.4% of RAM). A reservation is a promise, not use: big runtimes (Java, Go, browsers) and fork() reserve far more than they touch.

findings.title: Huge Pages
findings.explanation: Transparent huge pages are set to 'madvise': only programs that explicitly ask for huge pages get them. This is the safe middle ground and what most distributions recommend for servers. Right now 96.0 GB of program memory sits on huge pages.
